title: Spline-based prefill/decode scheduler with attention budgeting
creator: Aisha Mendez
description:
Problem: Our current prefill/decode schedulers use coarse heuristics (phase split by token counts or static tenant weights) which cause two observed issues: (1) short interactive requests suffer latency spikes when they get batched into heavy-attention kernels; (2) long-running throughput workloads occasionally starve latency-sensitive tenants during microburst windows.

Proposal: Implement a spline-based estimator + attention budget allocator in the scheduler. The estimator uses a compact profile trained from recent inference traces to predict attention compute cost across the next N tokens (per-request). We fit a low-degree spline over position vs attention-cost samples per model-variant and use that to find natural phase-split points where predicted marginal cost increases. The budget allocator assigns each request a small attention budget (in attention-ops units) derived from tenant SLA and recent utilization; the scheduler then prefers phase splits and kernel selections that keep estimated per-request attention under that budget while preserving aggregate throughput.

Key behaviors: 
- Dynamic phase splitting: split long requests at spline-inferred inflection points rather than fixed token counts.
- Kernel hinting: scheduler emits a kernel preference tag (e.g., "fast-low-attn" or "high-throughput") with each scheduled phase; runtime can use that to pick a quantized kernel path or lookup optimized kernel variant.
- Budgeted fairness: tenants accrue attention credits over time proportional to their SLA tier and recent underutilization; deficits reduce scheduling priority but do not block critical-short requests (latency hedge).
- Hedged fallback: if kernel selection fails due to placement/affinity, the scheduler will (optionally) reshuffle phase boundaries to maintain latency SLOs by moving small prefix tokens to a hedged low-latency kernel.

Why unique: Using splines to find natural phase boundaries reduces artificial fragmentation and aligns kernel choice with actual attention cost curves. Combining that with an explicit attention-budget abstraction makes fairness decisions interpretable and tunable by SLO owners.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler can compute spline-based phase split points per request and emit kernel hint metadata to the runtime
End-to-end canary shows <= 5% regression in system throughput for baseline workloads while improving p95 latency for short requests by >= 8%
Budgeted fairness prevents >75% of observed starvation incidents in tenant QoS tests compared to current scheduler
No production-level incidents introduced during canary; observability panels capture per-tenant attention usage and split decisions
implementation_steps: 1) Add lightweight attention-cost sampler in the runtime to emit position vs cost points (opt-in, bounded sampling rate)
2) Implement spline fitter service in scheduler (C++/Rust module) that maintains per-model-variant spline profiles
3) Extend request metadata to include estimated-cost curve and kernel_hint field
4) Add attention-budget accounting store (per-tenant sliding window) and budget-to-priority mapping
5) Wire scheduler decision path: compute spline -> find split candidates -> evaluate budget constraints -> select kernel_hint and schedule phases
6) Build feature flag + canary gating and dashboarding for metrics
7) Run performance experiments, collect data, and iterate on heuristics
tests: Unit: spline fitter correctness on synthetic cost curves (edge-case inflection, flat, noisy)
Unit: kernel_hint propagation via RPC and correct runtime interpretation
Integration: scheduler + runtime on a small cluster validating hedged fallback path
Load: multi-tenant load test with mix of short chat requests and long streaming generation (compare baseline vs spline-scheduler)
Chaos: simulate kernel placement failures to ensure hedged fallback keeps latency SLOs
metrics_targets: Short-request p95 latency reduction target: >= 8% (measured across 0-64 token requests)
End-to-end throughput (tokens/sec) degradation cap: <= 5% for mixed workload
Starvation incidents reduction: >= 75% fewer tenant starvation flags in stress tests
Scheduler CPU overhead: increase <= 3% on scheduler hosts (spline compute + accounting)
notes: Related: kernel-selection telemetry work (ENG-331200) — we need an agreed kernel taxonomy for hints
Model profiling job: data collected for gpt-lite-30b and open-13b on region-east-1 — stored in s3://redwood-profiling/2025/03
